answer: Yes. When you create a TOM with 'add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>', the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created along with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. required-type is mandatory on add and takes CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Optional attributes on add/set are required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (false/true, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; CHM7 cards only). Example: add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD

Use 'show tom-type-<tom-type> [data-rate] [description] [support-third-party-toms] [generic-subtype]'. The support-third-party-toms attribute is a boolean (false/true) that says whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to the supported Nokia TOMs. The companion attribute generic-subtype gives the 3rd party subtype string for that TOM, data-rate gives the approximate rate as uint16 in Gbps, and description is a human readable string (0..255). 'show tom-type' with no AID lists all supported types. The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the TOM itself, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) exists specifically to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It shows up under 'show unprovisioned-inventory', which lists detected inventory that the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration has not yet accepted. The AID form is unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>; chassis-serial-number is a string 0..16 and slot-name is a string 0..16, left empty when the equipment is the chassis itself. Retrievable attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (string 1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format, and detection-timestamp, which is the last time the Node Controller detected that unprovisioned equipment. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Run 'show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]', for example 'show usb-1-5-U1'; plain 'show usb' lists every USB port in the node with its type and present state. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted, a string 0..32, and it can be used as the target or source for file transfer operations. available-space is the current free space and total-space the total space, both uint16 in MB. All three of usb-path, available-space and total-space apply only when type is storage; the other role is power-supply, which powers external equipment such as passive shelves. present (true/false, default false) indicates whether the connector is inserted.

Use 'activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]' from Operational mode. db-instance names the snapshot to activate and defaults to temp; paraphrase is a short description of the database being activated, a string of length 40...200; sanity-check-override takes true or false and defaults to false, and is used to override the sanity check. The stated pre-condition is that a snapshot must already have been taken, with the related take-snapshot command. Examples given are 'activate-snapshot sanity-check-override' and 'activate-snapshot onehour'. Existing snapshots can be listed with 'show database'.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after 'enable-advanced-parameters' on the optical carrier is set to true. Two documented behaviours explain what you are seeing: if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter was deleted, 'show advanced-parameter' reports 'ERROR: object does not exist'; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value the configuration is not rejected, but 'show advanced-parameter' reports status 'failed' for it. The AID is advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name>, with add/set/show/delete. status values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set and unknown, default unknown.

Use 'apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*])' in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Set template-type to serdes-template, which applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in applicable-tom; if you do not supply applicable-tom, all system TOMs are considered for template application. Example: 'apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1'. This matters because 'set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates enabled' does not retroactively apply templates: on enabling, templates are applied only from that moment onward, so apply-template is how you push them onto already-installed pluggables. Disabling use-serdes-templates has no impact; existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs.

Yes, use a confirmed commit. From Candidate Configuration mode, entered with 'configure', run 'commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]'. The candidate configuration is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses, the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a persist trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. You confirm with 'commit persist' and abort with 'commit cancel'. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit the commands must carry the -id parameter, which ties commit confirmed, commit persist and commit cancel together. 'commit -m=<message>' attaches a custom message to a commit.

Use 'show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]' and pipe it through the display command: 'show config | display commands', then store the result for later use. That is the documented way to create a CLI script that can restore the system configuration. 'show config' displays only non-default configuration, skipping anything left at its default value, and the output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. To narrow the scope, supply an entity-id (the instance ID of one entity) or an entity-type when all entities of that type are relevant.

It depends on the target you pick. 'configure <target>' takes exclusive or shared, and defaults to exclusive. In exclusive mode only your session can make changes to the candidate configuration; in shared mode multiple sessions can change it concurrently. The command runs from Operational mode and moves you into Candidate Configuration mode. By default the candidate datastore starts as a copy of the running datastore, but you can change the starting point with 'from-default' for a blank config from scratch, 'from-script=<script>' to import configuration from a text file of CLI commands, or 'from-commit=<commit-id>' to initialize from a past commit record. from-commit is only available when the Commit Repository feature is available, that is when the commit-tracking system-policy is enabled. Example: configure exclusive

Use 'show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]', which shows the current values of the advanced parameters actually running on the system, as opposed to 'show advanced-parameter', which reports what you configured plus its status. Plain 'show current-advanced-parameter' lists them all; a wildcard form such as 'show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*' limits output to one optical carrier. Attributes are optical-carrier-name and current-advanced-parameter-name, both strings, and value, a string holding the running value. Typical entries include BOASetting, CRAvgNCtrl, ClockPreEmphasis, EEPNNLMitigation, FastCDAcqTimeCtrl, NLC, PDLMitigation, RxCDCompCtrl, RxCDMode and TxSignalBWControl. Note that PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. 'clear [-f] database' performs a full wipe of the database contents, sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, and is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity to the system. It does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data; use the 'clear system' command when you need a secure wipe or factory default. clear-type takes full (reset to factory defaults, the default), keep-networking (full wipe but network configurations are kept) or initialize-from-script (full wipe then initialize from a pre-stored .cli script). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. Expect transient alarms after the controller card reboot; these should be ignored. -f forces the command without confirmation.

Run 'db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>' from Operational mode with type set to encryption-with-integrity; the other permitted value is encryption. The example given is 'db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity', which enables the integrity check for the system database and automatically reboots the controller. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. The resulting protection scheme is visible with 'show db-protection-scheme', whose mode attribute reads encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and is documented as changeable via the db-migrate RPC. With integrity enabled the integrity-algorithm becomes hmac-sha2-512 rather than none, and integrity-status moves off disabled.

Run 'show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]' in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode and read integrity-status, which reports passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled. The other attributes are encryption-algorithm, which is xts-aes-256-plain64, AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size; integrity-algorithm, either hmac-sha2-512 or none; and mode, the current protection scheme of the DB, either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. On a node that has not been migrated the output reads integrity-algorithm none, integrity-status disabled, mode encryption-only.

Use 'diff [-t|-c] candidate', which must be run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the differences between the candidate datastore and the current system configuration as created, deleted or changed objects, showing only configurable attributes; 'new' data is the candidate and 'old' data is the current system configuration. Output forms: default normal diff style, where + marks added objects or new values and - marks deleted objects or old values; -t for a side-by-side table diff; -c to render the changes as CLI commands that reproduce the same configuration; and -d to list the commands being executed. So yes, 'diff -c candidate' gives you commands. 'diff commit <id> [<id>]' compares a commit record against the running configuration or another commit record, and is available when commit-tracking is enabled or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run 'discard-changes' from Candidate Configuration mode. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and no flags. Its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode only.

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care. It requires that you already know the extended-config name, and the name must match a name known by the system. The commands are 'add extended-config-<name>', 'delete extended-config-<name>' and 'show extended-config-<name> [description]', usable in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is a string of length 0..64. Before adding one, read the description attribute, a string of length 0..255 supplied by the system, which states what the extended-config is and its effect in the system.

Check the service-impact attribute in the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with 'show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> [description] [type] [supported-values] [direction] [multiplicity] [configuration-impact] [service-impact]'. service-impact is read-only and reads service-affecting or non-service-affecting; if it is service-affecting you must perform an admin lock or maintenance operation, or other relevant operations, before applying the change. configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change: no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change or full-config-no-pll-change. Also read supported-values for the allowed ranges or discrete numbers, multiplicity for how many values you must enter, and direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive). Example: show golden-advanced-parameter-chm7/EEPNNLMitigation

Run 'lock' (flag -h shows help) from Operational mode. It locks database access to the current session and grants that session exclusive write access, intended for holding configuration mastership for a short time. While the database is locked, any other session, CLI or otherwise, that tries to make a configuration change receives an error, and a lock is not possible if another session already holds one. The lock is released either by 'unlock' or by the locking session closing, whether the user closes it explicitly, an administrator closes it, or it hits the inactivity time-out. Only the session that took the lock can unlock it; unlocking a non-locked database, or one locked by another session, fails. After the unlock any session can configure again or take a new lock.

A named-value-set is addressed as named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>, where db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for that set. It holds a single 'value' item, a string of length 1..1024 characters. The commands are 'add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>]', 'set ... [value <value>]', 'show ... [value]' and 'delete ...'. All four are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

That depends on the restore-from-chassis-storage setting, shown and changed with 'show recovery' and 'set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value>'. Values are disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration on this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, then a manual clear recovery-mode is required, which lets you validate the restored system before affecting the HW), and auto-in-service (SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on successful restore the NC automatically leaves recovery mode). The default is auto-in-service, so with defaults it does pick the configuration up by itself. 'show recovery' also reports restore-status (init, image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore), backup-status (successful, failed, in-progress, unknown), last-backup and next-backup.

Only if the candidate is empty. 'rollback commit [<commit-id>]' works in the Running Datastore by default or in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if it is empty, which is in fact a way to initialize the candidate. If you omit the commit-id, the most recent commit record is used. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse commands for each record, and replays them in order from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit record. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

'show commit' is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither holds on your node, there is no Commit Repository to visualize. Turn it on with 'set system-policies commit-tracking enabled'; the default for commit-tracking is disabled. Note that disabling the policy again clears the commit-repository of all commit records. The syntax is 'show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>]', where <id> selects one specific commit record, -s picks a timestamp and shows all records created since it, and -n selects an exact number of records. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'set system-policies [commit-tracking <value>] [writable-running <value>]' and 'show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. commit-tracking enables the commit-repository feature, so all configuration changes made through the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit records that can be visualized, compared and rolled back; values enabled or disabled, default disabled. Disabling it clears the commit-repository of all commit records. writable-running is also enabled/disabled with default disabled; disabling the writable-running policy makes it impossible to configure via the running datastore, forcing use of the candidate: CLI allows add/set/delete only in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the candidate, and RESTCONF, gNMI (telemetry still allowed, gNOI still allowed), WebGUI and TL1 all become read-only.

The db-passphrase is missing. The system only accepts 'take-snapshot' if the db-passphrase used for DB snapshot encryption is configured, either globally as part of security-policies with 'set security-policies db-passphrase', or locally as a parameter, for example 'take-snapshot db-passphrase=***'. The passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and may use special characters from the 85-character Z85 set. Automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Syntax is 'take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]' from Operational mode. db-instance takes temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; description is a string 0...128. Re-taking an existing instance overwrites the existing file.
